The BlizzCon Collection consists of the optional virtual goodies from BlizzCon that are provided for those who purchase a BlizzCon ticket and as an optional purchase for those at home. Prior to 2021, the goodies were part of the Virtual Ticket which gave a front row seat at the convention from the comfort of ones own couch, live and in high definition. They got comprehensive coverage of both days of the show, including panels, contests, interviews, the closing ceremony, and more, along with some cool commemorative in-game goodies and the show was available to stream through the free BlizzCon Mobile app.

The Blizzard Feedback Tool is an official AddOn that can be found in clients used for testing new content, such as the Beta and Public Test Realm. It is used to report three different types of feedback to the Blizzard Quality Assurance Team in an organized fashion. The main button can be found around the minimap frame and uses a blue "B" as a symbol while tooltips for spells and items displayed a blue text stating to "ALT+Left Click for Feedback" (binding was adjustable). It isn't clear how long this addon was used, but it appeared at least as early as 19 June 2008 between patch 2.4.2 and patch 2.4.3. The BlizzCon Blink Store is only available for the upcoming weeks before a new BlizzCon convention as it gives BlizzCon attendees a way to make an online purchase and later pick up the merchandise at the convention while Blizzard Gear Store remains as a way to ship the merchandise. It made its first appearance with BlizzCon 2023.

The BlizzCon Guild Clash was a three-event tournament that took place on 4 November (the second day) of BlizzCon 2023. The three events consisted of 3v3 Arena PvP, 5v5 Mythic Dungeon Races, and a showcase event to wrap up the show. The last event was later revealed to be a raid showcase of Amirdrassil, the Dream's Hope coming with patch 10.2.0 and the competitors had to face four bosses from the raid which consisted of Gnarlroot, Igira the Cruel, Smolderon, and Tindral Sageswift. The four competitors included Echo, Method, Golden Guardians, and Team Liquid.

The Blizzard Fan Site Program was a program for fan sites officially recognized by Blizzard Entertainment. The program would last up to before the release of which was then discontinued. Blizzard_Menu is a new framework for creating context menus and dropdown menus, and is a complete replacement for UIDropDownMenu. All uses of UIDropDownMenu have been converted to use Blizzard_Menu, and UIDropDownMenu is now deprecated. Due to the large fundamental differences between these two systems, shims have not been provided, and any public uses of UIDropDownMenu will also need to rewrite their implementation in terms of Blizzard_Menu to take advantage of the changes.

The BlizzCon Invitational was a series of esports tournaments held during BlizzCon from 2007 to 2010, featuring players in Blizzard Entertainment titles. The inaugural event in 2007 introduced the format with competitive matches in Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne, including a $17,500 USD prize pool and international participants. Subsequent invitationals in 2008 and 2009 expanded and refined the brackets and increased visibility, while also showcasing StarCraft: Brood War as a parallel competitive title. The final BlizzCon Invitational in 2010 marked the transition toward StarCraft II esports and broader tournament formats, concluding the series' focused run on curated, invitation-only compe

The Blizzard Classic Cup is a multi-title esports showcase introduced at BlizzCon 2026, celebrating Blizzard Entertainment's legacy games through curated team competitions and community-driven formats. The inaugural Classic Cup will feature competitive brackets in Warcraft III: Reforged, StarCraft: Remastered, StarCraft II, and Heroes of the Storm. Warcraft III will mark its return to BlizzCon esports for the first time since the 2010 BlizzCon Invitational, with a dedicated offline tournament hosted on patch 2.0.3a.

Blizzard Entertainment SAS (previously Blizzard Entertainment Europe) was established in Paris, France in 2004 which handled the publishing and distribution operations, and Battle.net and game services in most countries in . Originally starting as a customer support division, World of Warcraft was the first non-licensed MMORPG in Europe to have the support of a dedicated local team from this location. In April 2009, the name was changed to Blizzard Entertainment SAS as all European publishing and distribution operations moved from the United States to this location.
